title: How Long Does a Generator Last? Run Hours and Years by Type
metaDescription: A portable generator lasts about 1,000 to 2,000 run hours and a home standby unit 10,000 to 30,000; here is each type in years, plus what shortens it.
h1: How Long Does a Generator Last?
keyword: how long does a generator last
keywords: how long does a generator last
intro:
A portable generator typically lasts 1,000 to 2,000 run hours (about 10 to 15 years of occasional use), and a home standby unit 10,000 to 30,000 hours (20 to 30 years). Here is each type, what wears it out early, and when to repair or replace.

Most portable generators last about 1,000 to 2,000 run hours, quality inverter models often reach 3,000 to 5,000, and home standby units are commonly rated for 10,000 to 30,000 hours, which works out to 20 years or more in a typical home. Engine design and maintenance decide where yours lands.

sections.heading: How Long Does a Generator Last? The Short Answer
sections.body:
**Short answer:** a mid-range portable generator typically lasts 1,000 to 2,000 run hours, a quality inverter 3,000 to 5,000, an air-cooled home standby unit 10,000 to 20,000 and a liquid-cooled standby unit 20,000 to 30,000 or more. In years of ordinary outage use that is roughly 10 to 15 years for a portable and 20 to 30 for standby. Maintenance, not the brand, decides where in that range yours lands.

Generators are rated in engine run hours, the same way a tractor or a boat motor is. A run hour is one hour with the engine turning, whether it powers a fridge or nothing at all. The calendar matters much less than how many of those hours the machine piles up and how well it was looked after while it did. That is why two generators bought the same year can be at opposite ends of their lives a decade later.

The figures below are the ranges manufacturers, dealers and service shops commonly cite. They are not guarantees, and no maker publishes a hard expiry date. Think of them as the point where a well-kept engine typically needs major work, such as a rebuild, rather than the moment it stops. Plenty of engines go past the top of the range; neglected ones fall well short of the bottom.

| Type | Typical run hours | Typical years in home use | Engine design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Budget open-frame portable | 500 to 1,000 | 5 to 10 | Small air-cooled, often no oil filter |
| Mid-range portable | 1,000 to 2,000 | 10 to 15 | Air-cooled OHV, splash lubrication |
| Quality inverter | 3,000 to 5,000 | 15 to 20 | Commercial-grade small engine, runs at variable speed |
| Air-cooled home standby | 10,000 to 20,000 | 20 to 30 | Pressure-lubricated V-twin with oil filter |
| Liquid-cooled standby | 20,000 to 30,000+ | 25 to 30+ | Automotive-style engine with radiator |

Budget open-frame portables sit at the bottom because they cut cost where it shows least on the shelf: thinner cylinder walls, no oil filter, plain bearings and minimal air filtration. They will run a fridge and a few lights through outages for years if the hours stay low, but a few long storm seasons can use them up. A mid-range portable from an established brand typically adds a cast-iron cylinder sleeve and better filtration, which is where the 1,000 to 2,000 hour range comes from.

Quality inverter generators last longer for two reasons. Their engines throttle down when the load is light instead of holding a fixed 3,600 rpm, so a half-loaded inverter wears more slowly per hour than a conventional portable. And the better brands use the same commercial engines sold for pumps and work equipment. Our [inverter generator guide](/best-inverter-generator/) lists which models carry that kind of engine.

Home standby generators are built for a different job entirely. They have pressure lubrication, a spin-on oil filter, a heavier block and an enclosure that keeps weather off the engine. Air-cooled units, the 10 to 26 kW machines most homes buy, are commonly rated in the 10,000 to 20,000 hour range. Liquid-cooled units, used for larger homes and light commercial work, run cooler and slower and are often quoted at 20,000 to 30,000 hours or more.

sections.heading: How Do Run Hours Translate Into Years?
sections.body:
Run hours only become years once you know how much you use the machine. A homeowner who runs a portable for two or three outages a year, maybe 30 to 60 hours in total, will take decades to use up a 1,500 hour engine. Long before then, the carburetor, fuel lines, recoil starter and battery will need attention. In light use, rubber parts and stale fuel usually end a portable's life before engine wear does.

A standby generator runs even when the power is on. Generac, Kohler and Briggs & Stratton units run a scheduled self-exercise, usually once a week for 5 to 20 minutes depending on model and setting, to keep the engine lubricated and the battery charged. At 12 minutes a week that is about 10 hours a year from exercise alone. Add a few days of outages and a typical home might log 50 to 150 hours a year, which is why 20 to 30 years is a realistic expectation for a maintained unit.

Rough Math for a Typical Home

~10 h

Yearly weekly-exercise hours (12 min)

50-150 h

Typical yearly total with outages

72 h

One three-day outage

20-30 yr

Common standby expectation

The math changes fast in areas with long outages. A single three-day outage is 72 hours. A week after a hurricane is 168. A homeowner on a rural line that drops for days several times a winter can put 400 or 500 hours a year on a machine. At that rate a 1,500 hour portable is worn out in three or four years, and even a standby unit will need its major service intervals far more often than the brochure suggests.

Most generators have an hour meter, and if yours does not, a clip-on meter costs very little. Knowing the real number changes every decision that follows: when to change oil, when to budget for a valve adjustment, and whether a used generator for sale is a bargain or someone else's worn-out engine. A seller who cannot tell you the hours is telling you something too.

Calendar age still matters on its own. Gaskets, fuel hoses, starter batteries and control boards age whether the engine runs or not. A standby unit that is 15 years old with only 1,500 hours on it may still need a new controller or transfer switch parts, simply because electronics and seals do not last forever outdoors. Plan for both clocks: engine hours for the motor, years for everything around it.

sections.heading: What Shortens a Generator's Life?
sections.body:
Old fuel is the most common killer of portable generators, by a wide margin. Gasoline with ethanol starts to break down in about a month, absorbing water and leaving varnish in the carburetor's tiny passages. The engine then surges, refuses to start or runs only on choke. Owners commonly report a generator that ran fine last storm season and will not start this one; in most of those cases the cause is fuel left in the carburetor over the summer.

Skipped oil changes come next. Small air-cooled engines run hot and hold very little oil, often less than a litre on a portable, so the oil breaks down quickly. Running a fresh engine through a long outage without the first break-in oil change is especially hard on it, because the metal particles from break-in stay in circulation. Low oil level is another trap: most generators have a low-oil shutdown, but running near the minimum still raises temperatures and wear.

Load matters in both directions. Running at or above the rated watts for hours makes the engine and alternator run hot and shortens both. Running a big conventional generator nearly empty for long periods is also unkind: the engine never reaches full temperature, and on larger engines this can lead to carbon build-up, sometimes called wet stacking on diesels. The sweet spot most manufacturers point toward is roughly 50 to 75 percent of rated output for long runs.

Dust, heat and weather wear generators down too. A generator run in a dusty yard with a clogged air filter ingests grit that scores the cylinder. One stored outdoors under a tarp corrodes its electrical connections and lets mice nest in the alternator. A standby unit installed where snow drifts over the air intake, or where lawn sprinklers soak it daily, ages faster than the same unit placed on a pad with clearances the manual specifies.

THE RULE

Fuel, oil and storage decide most generator lifespans.

Engines rarely wear out from honest hours. They die from varnished carburetors, cooked oil and seasons spent wet. Fix those three and most generators reach the top of their range.

sections.heading: What Maintenance Keeps a Generator Running Longest?
sections.body:
Your owner's manual is the authority, and intervals differ by brand and engine, so treat the schedule below as the shape most manuals follow rather than a replacement for yours. The common thread is that small engines need oil much more often than a car does. For a portable, many manuals call for the first oil change after a short break-in of roughly 5 to 25 hours, then every 50 to 100 hours or once a season, whichever comes first.

| Task | Portable / inverter | Home standby |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Break-in oil change | First 5 to 25 hours, per manual | Per dealer, often at first service |
| Routine oil change | Every 50 to 100 hours or yearly | Every 100 to 200 hours or yearly to every 2 years |
| Air filter | Clean every 50 hours, replace yearly | Replace at annual service |
| Spark plug | Check yearly, replace about every 100 to 300 hours | Replace at scheduled service |
| Fuel | Stabilize or run dry before storage | Natural gas or propane, no stale fuel |
| Exercise | Run 15 to 30 minutes monthly under load | Automatic weekly exercise |

Fuel care is where portables live or die. Either add a fuel stabilizer to every can and run the engine a few minutes so treated fuel reaches the carburetor, or run the carburetor dry before storage. Many owners do both. Stabilizer makers rate their products to keep gasoline usable for 12 to 24 months, which is far longer than untreated fuel lasts. Ethanol-free gasoline, where you can buy it, removes most of the water problem.

Run a portable once a month for 15 to 30 minutes with something plugged in. A space heater or a work light is enough. This keeps seals wet, charges the starter battery on electric-start models, and shows up problems while there is still time to fix them before a storm. Dual-fuel owners can run the monthly test on propane, which does not go stale, and keep the gasoline system dry until an outage. Our [gas generator guide](/best-gas-generator/) covers which models make that easy.

Standby generators should get an annual service from a dealer or a qualified technician: oil and filter, air filter, spark plugs, a battery test, a valve check on the schedule the maker specifies, and a look at the transfer switch. Generac's service guidance, for example, sets intervals by hours and by time, whichever comes first. The weekly exercise only proves the engine starts. It does not check oil condition or whether the transfer switch moves the house over properly under load.

Keep a log. A notebook taped inside the cover or a note on your phone with dates, hours and what was done will be worth money when you sell or claim warranty. Several manufacturers require proof of scheduled maintenance for warranty claims on engines, and a log is the simplest proof there is.

sections.heading: What Are the Signs a Generator Is Near the End?
sections.body:
Hard starting on its own is not a sign of old age. Nine times out of ten it is fuel, a fouled plug or a weak battery, all cheap fixes. The signs that point at a worn engine are different: blue smoke from the exhaust, oil consumption that climbs between changes, a noticeable drop in power under the same load, and knocking or rattling from inside the block. Together those usually mean worn rings, cylinder or bearings.

Electrical symptoms point at the alternator or the controls. Voltage that wanders, lights that pulse under steady load, breakers that trip at loads the generator used to carry easily, or an inverter that throws faults can all mean failing windings, a bad voltage regulator or a dying inverter module. On a conventional portable, an alternator rebuild or brush replacement is sometimes economical; on an inverter, the electronics module is often a large share of the machine's price.

Physical decay counts too. Cracked fuel lines, a rusted-through frame, a fuel tank that weeps at the seams and a recoil starter that has been replaced twice all add up. None of them is fatal alone, but together they say the machine has been outdoors a long time. On standby units, the enclosure, the controller and the transfer switch contacts are worth inspecting after 15 years even if the engine still sounds healthy.

Pay attention to what the generator does at full load, because that is when an outage tests it. A machine that idles smoothly but bogs down or stalls when the well pump or the furnace blower kicks in is not reliable backup any more. If you depend on the generator for medical equipment, a sump pump or heat, a load check once a year is the cheapest insurance you can buy.

Finally, look up parts availability. A generator from a brand that has left the market, or a model whose control board is no longer stocked, can be killed by a single failed part even when the engine has thousands of hours left. Mainstream brands with large dealer networks keep parts available for many years, which is part of why their machines last longer in practice.

sections.heading: Should You Repair or Replace an Old Generator?
sections.body:
A simple rule works for most portables: if a repair costs more than about half the price of a comparable new generator, replace it. Carburetor cleaning or replacement, spark plugs, fuel lines, a battery and a recoil starter are all cheap and almost always worth doing. Engine rebuilds, alternator rewinds and inverter modules usually are not on a budget portable, because the new machine also arrives with a fresh warranty.

Standby generators flip that math. The generator itself is often only a third to half of the installed cost; the rest is the transfer switch, gas line, electrical work, pad and permits, which you do not pay for again when you repair. Our [Generac generator cost breakdown](/generac-generator-cost/) shows how the line items split. A major engine repair on a standby unit can make sense well into its second decade, as long as parts are still available and the controller is supported.

Age of the technology matters as well. A 20-year-old standby generator may lack features newer ones have, such as smart load management that lets a smaller unit run central air, remote monitoring, and quieter exercise cycles. If your home's needs have grown, with an EV charger, a heat pump or a home office, an old unit may be both worn and undersized. In that case replacing it is an upgrade, not just a repair avoided.

The transfer switch deserves its own look. Automatic transfer switches on standby systems and manual switches or interlocks on portable setups often outlast one generator and serve the next. If you are replacing a portable, check that your new generator's outlet and wattage match your existing switch or inlet. Our [transfer switch guide](/best-generator-transfer-switch/) covers which switches suit which generators.

| Problem | Usually repair | Usually replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Won't start after storage | Yes: carburetor, plug, fuel | No |
| Dead starter battery | Yes | No |
| Blue smoke, burning oil | Standby: often yes | Budget portable: yes |
| Inverter module failure | Premium inverter: maybe | Budget inverter: yes |
| Rusted frame and tank | Rarely | Yes |

sections.heading: How Do You Buy a Generator That Lasts?
sections.body:
Look at the engine before the wattage. A cast-iron cylinder sleeve, an overhead-valve design, a low-oil shutdown and, on bigger machines, an oil filter are the features that separate a 1,000-hour engine from a 3,000-hour one. Manufacturers that sell their engines separately for commercial equipment tend to put the same engines in their generators, and their spec sheets say so.

Read the warranty as a signal of what the maker expects. Residential portable warranties commonly run two to three years, and premium inverter brands often sit at the top of that range. Standby generator warranties are typically five years limited for residential use, with some brands offering extended plans; Kohler, for example, has quoted residential terms in years and hours. Check the current terms on the maker's site before you buy, because they change, and note any hour caps and registration requirements.

Size it so it runs at half to three-quarters load during your normal outage. A generator that strains at its limit every time the furnace starts will wear faster than one with headroom, and a monster unit that idles near empty wastes fuel. Our [outage generator guide](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) walks through sizing from your actual loads. Fuel choice matters too: propane and natural gas do not go stale, which removes the biggest cause of early failure.

Plan storage before you buy. A portable that lives in a dry shed or garage, away from the car and its exhaust, with a cover and a fuel plan, will outlast an identical one left under a tarp. For a standby unit, placement on a raised pad with the clearances the manual specifies, away from sprinklers and drifting snow, gives the enclosure and electronics their best chance at 20-plus years.

Buy from a brand with a parts network near you. Being able to order a carburetor or a controller board quickly is the difference between a two-day fix and a dead machine. That is the quiet advantage of the big names, and it is a better predictor of real-world lifespan than any single number on the box.

mistakes.title: Storing Untreated Gas in the Carburetor
mistakes.body: Ethanol fuel starts breaking down within weeks and varnishes the carburetor's small jets. This is the single most common reason portables refuse to start after a summer in the garage. Add stabilizer and run it through, or run the carburetor dry before storage.

mistakes.title: Skipping the Break-In Oil Change
mistakes.body: A new engine sheds metal particles during its first hours. Many manuals call for the first oil change after roughly 5 to 25 hours for exactly this reason. Running a fresh generator through a long outage on factory oil starts its life with avoidable wear.

mistakes.title: Never Running It Between Outages
mistakes.body: A generator that sits for a year dries out seals, lets the battery die and hides problems until the night you need it. A monthly 15 to 30 minute run under some load keeps it ready and catches issues while repairs are still easy.

mistakes.title: Running at Full Load for Days
mistakes.body: Pulling the full rated watts for long periods overheats the engine and alternator. Size the machine so normal outage loads sit around half to three-quarters of its rating, and stagger big motor loads like well pumps and air conditioners.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the Hour Meter
mistakes.body: Oil intervals, valve checks and resale value all depend on run hours, not months. Owners who never read the meter tend to change oil too late after a long outage. Check it after every outage and log the number with the date.

faqs.q: How many hours will a portable generator last?
faqs.a: Most mid-range portable generators are commonly rated around 1,000 to 2,000 run hours before needing major engine work, while budget open-frame units often sit closer to 500 to 1,000. Quality inverter models built on commercial-grade engines are frequently quoted at 3,000 to 5,000 hours. Maintenance and fuel care move a machine toward the top or bottom of its range.

faqs.q: How many years does a whole-house generator last?
faqs.a: A maintained home standby generator commonly lasts 20 to 30 years. Air-cooled units are usually rated for about 10,000 to 20,000 hours and liquid-cooled units for 20,000 to 30,000 or more. Because a typical home logs only 50 to 150 hours a year, calendar wear on electronics, seals and the battery often matters as much as engine hours.

faqs.q: Is 1,000 hours a lot for a generator?
faqs.a: It depends on the type. On a budget portable, 1,000 hours is near the end of its expected engine life. On a quality inverter it is roughly a quarter of the way through, and on a home standby unit it is barely broken in. Ask what maintenance was done during those hours before judging a used machine by the number alone.

faqs.q: How often should a generator be serviced?
faqs.a: Portables typically need an oil change every 50 to 100 hours or once a season, plus air filter and spark plug checks; the first change comes after a short break-in period. Standby units usually get an annual professional service covering oil, filters, plugs, battery and the transfer switch. Always follow the intervals in your own owner's manual.

faqs.q: Does running a generator without load hurt it?
faqs.a: Short no-load runs, such as a standby generator's weekly exercise, are normal and do no harm. Long periods at very light load are less ideal on larger engines because they never reach full operating temperature, which can encourage carbon build-up. For monthly test runs on a portable, plug in a modest load like a work light or space heater.

faqs.q: Can a generator sit for years and still work?
faqs.a: It can, if it was stored properly: carburetor run dry or fuel stabilized, fresh oil, battery on a maintainer and kept somewhere dry. Generators stored with untreated gasoline usually need carburetor cleaning before they will run. Expect to replace the battery and check fuel lines on any machine that has sat for several years.

faqs.q: Do inverter generators last longer than regular ones?
faqs.a: Quality inverter generators often do, for two reasons. Their engines slow down at light loads instead of holding a fixed 3,600 rpm, so they accumulate less wear per hour, and premium brands use commercial-grade engines. Budget inverters do not always share those advantages, so check the engine specification and warranty rather than assuming.

bottomLine:
A generator lasts as long as its engine design allows and its owner lets it. Budget portables are built for hundreds of hours, good portables for one to two thousand, quality inverters for several thousand, and standby units for tens of thousands. Within each range, fuel care, oil changes and dry storage decide whether you get the low number or the high one.

If your current machine is struggling, start with the cheap fixes: fresh fuel, a cleaned carburetor, a new plug and a charged battery. If it is genuinely worn out, size the replacement to your real loads and buy the engine, warranty and parts network that match how long you want it to last.
